title: Laptop hardware: what's different and why it matters
summary: SODIMM, M.2, and the parts you'll actually be asked to replace.
body:
## A laptop is a desktop with every constraint turned up

Everything in a laptop is shaped by three pressures a desktop never feels: space, heat, and battery. Once you know that, most laptop-specific exam answers follow logically rather than needing memorisation.

### Memory: SODIMM, not DIMM

Laptops use **SODIMM** (Small Outline DIMM) modules — physically shorter than the DIMMs in a desktop and not interchangeable with them. The generation still matters exactly as it does on a desktop: DDR4 and DDR5 SODIMMs are keyed differently and will not fit each other's slots, which is deliberate, because they run at different voltages and would be damaged.

Two things trip people up in practice:

- Many thin laptops now **solder** some or all memory to the board. If a machine ships with 8 GB soldered and one open slot, the maximum is 8 GB plus whatever that slot accepts — not double the installed amount.
- Some laptops run **single-channel** unless both slots are populated. Adding a second matched module can measurably improve integrated-graphics performance, because the GPU is sharing that same memory bandwidth.

> Exam habit: if a question gives you a laptop model's maximum RAM and the current configuration, check whether the installed memory is soldered before assuming both slots are free.

### Storage: the M.2 keying question

Modern laptops use **M.2** modules, and the keying determines what actually works:

| Form factor | Interface | Practical speed |
|---|---|---|
| M.2 **M-key** | PCIe (NVMe) | Fastest — several GB/s |
| M.2 **B-key** | Usually SATA | Capped at SATA III, about 6 Gbps |
| 2.5-inch drive | SATA | About 6 Gbps, thicker, older designs |
| mSATA | SATA | Legacy predecessor to M.2 |

An M-keyed slot carrying PCIe lanes is the fast option. A slot that only speaks SATA gives you SATA speeds no matter how expensive the drive is, which is why "the new NVMe drive isn't any faster" is usually a slot-capability problem rather than a faulty drive.

### The display assembly is a subsystem, not a panel

When a lid is damaged, several components live inside it:

- The **LCD/LED panel** itself.
- The **digitizer**, on touch models — the transparent layer that senses touch. A cracked digitizer with an intact panel gives you a perfect picture that ignores your finger; a cracked panel with a working digitizer gives you touch input on a broken image. The exam likes this distinction.
- The **webcam and microphone array**.
- The **Wi-Fi antennas**, which run up the sides of the lid because that is the highest, least shielded point in the chassis. This is why Wi-Fi reception can degrade after a sloppy screen replacement — the antenna leads were pinched or left disconnected.
- The **inverter**, on older CCFL-backlit panels, which converts DC to the high-voltage AC the backlight tube needs. LED panels replaced it with a driver circuit.

That inverter detail produces one of the most reliable symptom questions on the exam: a display that is **very dim but shows a faint image under a bright flashlight** has a working panel and a failed backlight or inverter. The image is being produced; it just is not being lit.

### Power and batteries

Laptop batteries are lithium-ion, and two facts matter operationally. First, a **swollen battery is a safety hazard** — it must be removed from service immediately, never punctured, and disposed of through proper recycling, not general waste. A trackpad that has started clicking oddly or a case that no longer sits flat is often a swelling battery pushing from underneath.

Second, laptops negotiate charging over the power adapter. An underrated USB-C adapter may run the machine but charge slowly or not at all under load, which presents as "it only charges when powered off."

### Field-replaceable versus soldered

The practical service question is always what you can actually replace:

| Usually replaceable | Usually soldered or integrated |
|---|---|
| SODIMM memory (when slotted) | CPU |
| M.2 or 2.5-inch storage | Integrated GPU |
| Battery, keyboard, trackpad | Embedded controller and firmware chips |
| Wi-Fi card (M.2 A/E key) | On thin models, RAM and sometimes storage |
| Display assembly, hinges, ribbon cable | The board's soldered I/O controllers |

The hinge and the **display ribbon cable** deserve a special mention: they flex every single time the lid opens. They are the components most likely to fail mechanically on an otherwise healthy machine, producing intermittent flicker, lines, or a display that cuts out at a particular lid angle.

### Docking stations and port replicators

A **port replicator** adds ports. A **docking station** adds ports *and* power delivery, usually over a single USB-C or Thunderbolt connection, so the laptop attaches to a desk setup with one cable. On the exam, if a scenario mentions one cable providing display, network, peripherals, and charging, that is a dock.

> Exam habit: when a laptop symptom involves the lid — flicker, dimness, no touch, weak Wi-Fi — think through the display assembly's components before suspecting the motherboard. The lid contains far more than a screen.

title: Mobile connectivity: cellular, Bluetooth, and hotspots
summary: The radios in a phone and the settings that break them.
body:
## Mobile connectivity: matching the radio to the job

Phones and tablets carry several radios at once, and the exam tests whether you can pick the right one for a described scenario. Each exists because the others are wrong for that particular job.

### The four radios, by range and purpose

| Technology | Typical range | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **NFC** | A few centimetres | Tap-to-pay, pairing handshakes, transit cards |
| **Bluetooth** | About 10 metres | Peripherals: headsets, keyboards, watches, car audio |
| **Wi-Fi** | Tens of metres | High-bandwidth data on a local network |
| **Cellular** | Kilometres | Wide-area data and voice wherever there is coverage |

The short range of **NFC** is a security property, not a limitation. An attacker has to be essentially touching the device, which is exactly why it is acceptable for payments while Bluetooth would not be.

### Bluetooth pairing, and why it fails

Pairing requires three things: both devices powered, the accessory in **discoverable/pairing mode**, and the two within range. Most "it will not pair" tickets are one of those three, not a fault.

The sequence the exam expects is: enable Bluetooth, put the accessory into pairing mode, select it on the phone, confirm the PIN or passkey if prompted, then test. If a previously working device stops connecting, the standard fix is to **remove (forget) the pairing and re-pair**, which clears a stale key.

### Cellular generations and the standards underneath

You are not expected to recite modulation schemes, but you are expected to know the ordering and a couple of distinctions:

- **3G** — legacy data, largely retired.
- **4G LTE** — the baseline for modern data service.
- **5G** — highest throughput and lowest latency, with coverage that varies sharply by band. High-band ("mmWave") 5G is extremely fast over very short distances; low-band 5G travels far but is closer to LTE speeds.

Two older terms still appear: **GSM** networks used removable SIM cards and were the global standard, while **CDMA** networks historically tied the device to the carrier without a SIM. Modern devices have largely converged, and the practical descendant of that distinction is the **eSIM** — an embedded SIM provisioned by software, so a carrier can be switched without a physical card.

### Hotspot and tethering

**Tethering** shares a phone's cellular connection with another device. It can run over USB cable, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi; the Wi-Fi form is usually called a **mobile hotspot**. Three practical consequences the exam likes:

- It consumes the phone's cellular data allowance, and carriers frequently meter hotspot data separately from on-device data.
- It drains the battery quickly, because the phone is running two radios hard at once.
- Corporate policy often disables it through MDM, because it creates an unmanaged path around the corporate network.

### Airplane mode is a switch, not a setting

Airplane mode disables **all** radios at once. Its most common troubleshooting use is as a fast, reversible way to force every radio to reinitialise: toggle it on, wait a moment, toggle it off. That resolves a surprising share of "no signal" and "will not connect" complaints without a reboot.

Note that on modern devices Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can be re-enabled individually *while* airplane mode remains on, which is why "the user says airplane mode is on but Bluetooth still works" is not a fault.

### Configuring corporate email

For over-the-air mail sync, the technician needs the account credentials and the server details. For a manually configured account that means:

| Setting | What it controls |
|---|---|
| **Incoming server** (IMAP or POP3) | Where mail is read from |
| **Outgoing server** (SMTP) | Where mail is sent through |
| **Ports and security type** | Which port, and whether SSL/TLS is required |
| **Authentication** | Username, password, and whether the outgoing server also requires it |

Choose **IMAP** when the user reads mail on more than one device, because it keeps messages and folder state on the server so every device sees the same mailbox. **POP3** traditionally downloads and removes mail, which breaks multi-device use — that is the distinction the exam tests, not the port numbers alone.

Most corporate environments avoid all of this by using a synchronisation service that provisions mail, contacts, and calendar together from one account entry, often enforced through **MDM** so that the profile can be removed remotely when the person leaves.

### Mobile device management

**MDM** enrols a device under central policy. The capabilities that matter for exam scenarios are remote **lock**, remote **wipe**, enforcing a **screen lock and encryption**, pushing configuration profiles, and controlling which applications may be installed. On personally owned devices under a **BYOD** policy, MDM typically creates a managed container so corporate data can be wiped without touching the user's personal photos.

> Exam habit: for a lost device holding sensitive data, the first action is always to protect the data — remote wipe through MDM — not to file paperwork or order a replacement. Those come after.

title: Ports and protocols worth memorizing
summary: The port numbers A+ asks about, grouped so they stick.
body:
## Ports and protocols: learn them in groups, not as a list

A flat list of thirty port numbers is almost impossible to retain. Grouped by what they do, and paired with their secure counterparts, they stick — and the exam almost always asks which protocol fits a described need rather than reciting a number cold.

### Mail

| Protocol | Port | Job |
|---|---|---|
| SMTP | 25 | Sending mail between servers |
| SMTP submission (secured) | 587 | A mail client submitting outbound mail |
| POP3 | 110 | Retrieving mail, traditionally downloading and removing it |
| POP3S | 995 | POP3 wrapped in TLS |
| IMAP | 143 | Retrieving mail while leaving it on the server |
| IMAPS | 993 | IMAP wrapped in TLS |

The distinction that matters operationally: **SMTP sends, POP3 and IMAP retrieve**. If a user can receive but not send, look at the outgoing (SMTP) configuration; if they can send but not receive, look at the incoming side. And when a user has a phone and a laptop and wants both to show the same mailbox state, the answer is **IMAP**.

### Web and remote access

| Protocol | Port | Job |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | 80 | Unencrypted web |
| HTTPS | 443 | Web over TLS |
| SSH | 22 | Encrypted remote shell; also carries SFTP |
| Telnet | 23 | Remote shell in **cleartext** — legacy, avoid |
| RDP | 3389 | Windows graphical remote desktop |

**SSH replaced Telnet** for exactly one reason: Telnet transmits everything, including credentials, in readable text. Any question contrasting the two is testing that.

### File transfer

| Protocol | Port | Job |
|---|---|---|
| FTP | 20 and 21 | Data and control channels, unencrypted |
| SFTP | 22 | File transfer tunnelled over SSH |
| TFTP | 69 | Trivial FTP over UDP, no authentication — used for device firmware and network boot |
| SMB | 445 | Windows file and printer sharing |

TFTP's lack of authentication is the point: it is deliberately minimal so that a device with almost no software can pull a firmware image at boot. That also makes it unsuitable for anything sensitive.

### Infrastructure services

| Protocol | Port | Job |
|---|---|---|
| DNS | 53 | Resolves names to IP addresses |
| DHCP | 67 and 68 | Leases IP configuration to clients |
| NTP | 123 | Synchronises clocks |
| SNMP | 161 and 162 | Device monitoring: polling and traps |
| LDAP | 389 | Directory queries |
| LDAPS | 636 | LDAP over TLS |

**NTP looks unimportant until it breaks.** Kerberos authentication rejects tickets when clocks drift too far, TLS certificates appear invalid if the clock is wrong, and correlating logs across devices becomes impossible. A workstation that suddenly cannot log into the domain, with no other changes, is a classic clock-skew scenario.

### TCP versus UDP

This is the concept behind the port list, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising.

**TCP** establishes a connection with a three-way handshake, numbers its segments, acknowledges receipt, and retransmits anything lost. You get ordered, reliable delivery, at the cost of overhead and delay when retransmitting.

**UDP** simply sends. There is no handshake, no acknowledgement, and no retransmission. It is faster and has less overhead, and if a packet is lost it is simply gone.

That trade-off explains the assignments:

- **DNS queries** and **DHCP** use UDP because a single small exchange is cheaper to repeat than to negotiate a connection for.
- **Voice and video streaming** favour UDP because a retransmitted packet arriving late is useless — you would rather have a momentary glitch than the whole stream stalling to wait for it.
- **Web, file transfer, and email** use TCP because a document with missing pieces is worthless.

> Exam habit: when a question describes real-time media and asks which transport, the answer is UDP, and the justification is that late data is worse than missing data.

### Reading the secure-counterpart pattern

Notice how consistently the secure version is a different port running the same protocol inside TLS: HTTP 80 to HTTPS 443, LDAP 389 to LDAPS 636, IMAP 143 to IMAPS 993, POP3 110 to POP3S 995. If you know the plaintext port and recognise that pattern, you can reason your way to the secure one instead of memorising twice as many numbers.

title: IP addressing and what APIPA is telling you
summary: Private ranges, DHCP, and reading 169.254 as a diagnosis.
body:
## IP addressing, and reading an address as a diagnostic

An IP configuration is a status report. Once you can read one, a large share of connectivity tickets resolve themselves before you touch a cable.

### The four values every host needs

| Value | What it does | Symptom when wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **IP address** | Identifies the host on its network | Duplicate address, or no connectivity at all |
| **Subnet mask** | Says which part of the address is the network | Host cannot reach devices it should reach locally |
| **Default gateway** | Where to send traffic destined off-subnet | Local traffic works, internet does not |
| **DNS server** | Resolves names to addresses | Sites fail by name but work by IP |

That last row is the single most useful diagnostic split in the whole domain. If `ping 8.8.8.8` succeeds but `ping google.com` fails, routing and connectivity are fine and the problem is **name resolution**. You have isolated the fault to DNS without touching anything else.

### Private address ranges

RFC 1918 reserves three blocks that are never routed on the public internet:

| Range | CIDR | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255 | 10.0.0.0/8 | Large enterprise networks |
| 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 | 172.16.0.0/12 | Medium networks |
| 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 | 192.168.0.0/16 | Home and small office |

Note the 172 range carefully: it runs from 172.**16** to 172.**31**, not the whole 172 block. An address of 172.15.x.x or 172.32.x.x is public, and that is a favourite exam distractor.

Because these addresses cannot be routed publicly, a router performs **NAT** — rewriting the private source address to its own public address and tracking the session so replies come back to the right internal host. That is how an entire office shares one public IP.

### APIPA is the network telling you something

If a client is set to obtain an address automatically and gets **169.254.x.x**, that is **APIPA** — Automatic Private IP Addressing. The host asked for a DHCP lease, received no answer, and self-assigned.

An APIPA address means one thing: **the client could not reach a DHCP server.** The cause is upstream:

- The DHCP server is down or its scope is exhausted.
- A cable, switch port, or VLAN assignment is broken between client and server.
- The client is on a subnet whose router is not forwarding DHCP (no relay/IP helper configured).

Two hosts that both fell back to APIPA can actually talk to each other, since they are on the same 169.254.0.0/16 link-local network — but neither can reach the gateway or the internet. That is exactly the reported symptom: "I can see the other machine but nothing else works."

The other special address worth knowing is **127.0.0.1**, the loopback. Pinging it tests only that the local TCP/IP stack is installed and functioning; success tells you nothing whatsoever about cables, switches, or the network.

### Static versus dynamic assignment

**DHCP** hands out configuration automatically through a four-step exchange — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — and is the default for client devices because it scales and avoids conflicts.

**Static** addressing is assigned by hand and is appropriate where an address must never change: servers, printers, switches, and routers. The risk is human error — a statically assigned address that overlaps the DHCP scope produces an intermittent **duplicate IP address** conflict, where both devices work erratically and Windows raises an address-conflict warning.

The middle path is a **DHCP reservation**: the server always issues the same address to a specific MAC address. The device is configured for DHCP, so it can be managed centrally, but its address is predictable. For printers this is almost always the right answer.

### Subnet masks, without the maths panic

The mask separates the network portion from the host portion. For A+ purposes you mainly need to read the common ones:

| CIDR | Mask | Usable hosts |
|---|---|---|
| /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 254 |
| /25 | 255.255.255.128 | 126 |
| /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 62 |
| /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 2 |

Total addresses are 2 raised to the number of host bits; usable hosts are that minus two, because the first address identifies the network and the last is the broadcast address.

A **mismatched mask** creates a distinctive symptom: the host believes some addresses are local when they are not, so it tries to reach them directly instead of via the gateway. The result is that some destinations work and others fail with no obvious pattern.

### IPv6, briefly

IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal, which removes address exhaustion entirely and eliminates the need for NAT. You will see two forms:

- **Link-local**, beginning **fe80::**, self-configured on every interface and used only on the local segment. It is the IPv6 counterpart to APIPA in appearance, but unlike APIPA it is normal and expected, not a fault indicator.
- **Global unicast**, routable on the public internet.

> Exam habit: 169.254 means DHCP failed. fe80 does not — it is a normal part of every IPv6 interface, and its presence is not a symptom.

title: SOHO networks, VPNs, and the tools that diagnose them
summary: What a small office/home office network is made of, how a VPN fits in, and the tools that troubleshoot the wiring itself.
body:
## Building a small network, and proving it works

A SOHO install is the same handful of decisions every time: address the clients, secure the wireless, expose only what must be exposed, and be able to prove where a fault lies.

### What the all-in-one box is actually doing

The device most people call "the router" is usually four things at once:

- A **router**, moving traffic between the local network and the internet.
- A **switch**, giving the wired ports a local Layer 2 network.
- A **wireless access point**, bridging Wi-Fi clients onto that same network.
- A **firewall performing NAT**, which is what lets many private addresses share one public one.

Knowing that matters for troubleshooting: "wired works, wireless does not" points at the AP function, while "nothing reaches the internet but devices see each other" points at the router or the WAN link.

### Securing the wireless

The encryption ladder, worst to best:

| Standard | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **WEP** | Broken. Recoverable in minutes. Never deploy. |
| **WPA** | Deprecated; used TKIP as a stopgap for WEP-era hardware. |
| **WPA2** | AES-CCMP. Still acceptable. |
| **WPA3** | Current best; its SAE handshake resists offline password guessing. |

Beyond encryption, the settings that actually matter are changing the **default administrator credentials**, keeping **firmware updated**, and putting visitors on a **guest network** so they get internet without reaching internal file shares or printers.

Two commonly recommended measures are weaker than they look. **Hiding the SSID** stops it appearing in a casual scan, but the name is still broadcast in client traffic and trivially recovered. **MAC filtering** blocks casual connection, but MAC addresses travel in the clear and can be cloned. Treat both as speed bumps, never as the control.

### Port forwarding and the DMZ

By default NAT means unsolicited inbound traffic has nowhere to go. **Port forwarding** creates a deliberate exception: traffic arriving on a specified external port is sent to one internal host and port. That is how a game server or a security camera becomes reachable from outside.

Some consumer routers offer a **"DMZ host"** setting that forwards *all* unsolicited inbound traffic to one machine. This is not the screened subnet of enterprise design — it is a blunt instrument that exposes that host completely, and it should be avoided in favour of forwarding only the specific ports required.

**UPnP** lets applications open their own forwards without asking anyone. Convenient, and exactly why it is commonly disabled: malware on the network gets the same privilege.

### VPNs

A **VPN** builds an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network so a remote user can reach internal resources as though on site. Two shapes appear on the exam:

- **Client-to-site** (remote access): an individual device connects into the corporate network. This is the hotel and coffee-shop scenario.
- **Site-to-site**: two networks are joined permanently, typically branch office to head office, and users are unaware it exists.

There is also a configuration distinction worth carrying: a **full tunnel** sends all of the client's traffic through the corporate network, including ordinary web browsing, which allows inspection and filtering but consumes bandwidth. A **split tunnel** sends only corporate-bound traffic down the tunnel and lets the rest go direct — faster, but that traffic bypasses corporate inspection.

### The command-line tools that isolate a fault

These are how you convert a vague complaint into a located problem.

| Command | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `ipconfig /all` | What address, mask, gateway, and DNS does this host actually have? |
| `ping <gateway>` | Is the local path to the router working? |
| `ping 8.8.8.8` | Does routing to the internet work, independent of DNS? |
| `ping <name>` | Does name resolution work? |
| `tracert <host>` | Where along the path does it stop? |
| `nslookup <name>` | What is DNS actually returning for this name? |
| `netstat -ano` | What is listening or connected, and which process owns it? |
| `ipconfig /flushdns` | Clear cached DNS answers after a record change |

Run in that order, they narrow the fault methodically. Address looks wrong (169.254) — DHCP problem. Gateway pings but 8.8.8.8 does not — routing or ISP. 8.8.8.8 pings but the name does not — DNS. That single sequence resolves most connectivity tickets.

> Exam habit: `ping 8.8.8.8` versus `ping google.com` is the fastest way to split "no connectivity" from "no name resolution," and the exam expects you to reach for it.

title: Server roles, internet appliances, and legacy/embedded systems
summary: What each networked host actually does, matched to the acronym the exam names it by.
body:
## Naming the boxes on the rack, and the appliances in front of them

Objective 2.3 is largely vocabulary: given a described job, name the server role or appliance that does it. The trick is that several sound similar, so anchor each to the one job only it does.

### Core server roles

| Role | The job only it does |
|---|---|
| **DNS server** | Resolves names to IP addresses |
| **DHCP server** | Leases IP configuration to clients |
| **File server** | Central shared storage for documents |
| **Print server** | Manages shared printers and their queues |
| **Mail server** | Sends, receives, and stores email |
| **Web server** | Serves pages and web applications over HTTP/HTTPS |
| **Database server** | Stores structured data queried by applications |
| **Syslog server** | Centrally collects log messages from many devices |
| **NTP server** | Distributes accurate time |
| **AAA server** | Authentication, authorization, and accounting for network access |
| **Proxy server** | Makes requests on clients' behalf; caches and filters |

The **syslog server** is worth dwelling on. Collecting logs centrally is not just convenient — it is a security control. An attacker who compromises a host can clear that host's local log, but not the copy already shipped elsewhere. That is why "missing logs" is treated as evidence rather than a glitch.

**AAA** is the umbrella that RADIUS and TACACS+ implement: *authentication* proves who you are, *authorization* decides what you may do, and *accounting* records what you did.

### Network appliances

| Appliance | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Load balancer** | Spreads requests across several servers for capacity and resilience |
| **Proxy** | Intermediary for client requests — caching, filtering, hiding internal addresses |
| **Spam gateway** | Filters unwanted and malicious mail before it reaches users |
| **UTM** | Unified Threat Management: firewall, IPS, antivirus, filtering in one box |
| **IDS / IPS** | Detects suspicious traffic; an IPS sits inline and can block it |
| **Firewall** | Permits or denies traffic by rule |

The **IDS versus IPS** distinction is pure detection versus prevention. An IDS observes and alerts — it is out of the traffic path, so it cannot stop anything. An IPS sits **inline**, so it can drop the traffic, at the cost of becoming a potential point of failure and latency.

### Embedded, industrial, and legacy systems

Some systems are not general-purpose computers at all, and the exam expects you to recognise them:

- **SCADA / ICS** — Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition, and Industrial Control Systems: the equipment that runs physical processes in utilities, manufacturing, and building automation.
- **Embedded systems** — purpose-built computers inside another device: a thermostat, a medical pump, a point-of-sale terminal.
- **IoT devices** — network-connected consumer and building devices: cameras, doorbells, smart plugs.
- **Legacy systems** — older equipment kept running because replacing it is impractical, frequently past end-of-support.

These share one security answer, and the exam asks it repeatedly: **segment them onto their own network**. They often cannot be patched, run outdated software, and were not designed with security in mind. Isolation is the compensating control. A compromised smart thermostat should not be able to reach the finance server, and a factory-floor sensor should not be reachable from the general office network.

### Legacy protocols and why they persist

You will still encounter **Telnet** (unencrypted remote shell), plain **FTP**, and **SNMPv1/v2c** with cleartext community strings. Each has a secure replacement — SSH, SFTP, SNMPv3 — and the exam's position is consistent: use the secure version, and if legacy equipment genuinely cannot support it, isolate that equipment rather than accepting the exposure network-wide.

> Exam habit: when a question describes equipment that cannot be patched or updated, the expected answer is almost always network segmentation, not "install antivirus on it."

title: RAID levels and what each one is buying you
summary: 0, 1, 5, 10 — the trade between speed, redundancy, and capacity.
body:
## RAID: what each level actually buys you

Every RAID level trades among three things — capacity, speed, and fault tolerance. You cannot maximise all three, and the level names are just different points on that trade.

### The levels the exam tests

| Level | Minimum drives | Fault tolerance | Usable capacity | Character |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RAID 0** | 2 | **None** | 100% | Striping. Fast, and one drive lost means everything lost. |
| **RAID 1** | 2 | 1 drive | 50% | Mirroring. Simple, expensive per usable GB. |
| **RAID 5** | 3 | 1 drive | (n−1)/n | Striping with distributed parity. |
| **RAID 6** | 4 | **2 drives** | (n−2)/n | Like RAID 5 with a second parity block. |
| **RAID 10** | 4 | 1 per mirror | 50% | Mirrored pairs, then striped. Fast and resilient. |

### Reading the trade

**RAID 0** has no redundancy at all — the zero is a useful mnemonic for "zero protection." It stripes data across drives so reads and writes hit several spindles at once, which is genuinely fast, but the failure of any single drive destroys the whole array. It is appropriate only for scratch data you can afford to lose.

**RAID 1** writes everything twice. You lose half your raw capacity, but recovery is trivial: the surviving drive already holds a complete copy. It is common for boot volumes.

**RAID 5** is the classic capacity/protection compromise. Parity is distributed across all drives, so with n drives you get (n−1) drives' worth of usable space and survive one failure. Its weakness is the **rebuild window**: replacing a failed drive forces a read of every remaining drive to reconstruct the data, which is exactly when a second, already-stressed drive is most likely to fail. With large modern drives that rebuild can run for many hours.

**RAID 6** answers that weakness with a second parity block, surviving **two** simultaneous failures. It costs more capacity and writes more slowly, and it is the sensible choice for large arrays where rebuild times are long.

**RAID 10** combines both ideas: mirror pairs of drives, then stripe across those pairs. You get RAID 1's fast, simple rebuild — copy from the surviving mirror, no parity calculation — with striping's performance. You pay half your capacity for it, which is why it is favoured for databases and heavy write workloads where RAID 5's parity overhead hurts.

### The thing RAID is not

**RAID is not a backup.** It protects against a *drive* failing. It does nothing about:

- A file deleted by mistake — deleted on every drive instantly.
- Ransomware encrypting the volume — encrypted everywhere at once.
- A controller failure, fire, flood, or theft taking the whole array.
- Corruption written faithfully to every member.

This turns up constantly on the exam, phrased as a company that "has RAID so does not need backups." The answer is always that redundancy and backup solve different problems, and both are required.

### Hardware versus software RAID

**Hardware RAID** uses a dedicated controller with its own processor and often a battery-backed cache. It is faster and invisible to the operating system, but the array is typically tied to that controller family — a dead controller may require a compatible replacement to read the array.

**Software RAID** is implemented by the operating system. It costs some CPU, but it is portable between machines and requires no special hardware.

### Reading a failure scenario

When a question describes an array, work through it in order:

1. How many drives failed?
2. Which level is it, and how many failures does that level tolerate?
3. Is the array degraded (running, protection reduced) or failed (data lost)?

A RAID 5 with one failed drive is **degraded** — still serving data, with no remaining protection, and replacing that drive is now urgent. The same array with two failed drives has lost the data, and the answer is restore from backup.

> Exam habit: match the requirement to the minimum level that satisfies it. "Survive one drive failure with good capacity efficiency" is RAID 5. "Survive two" is RAID 6. "Fastest with redundancy, capacity is not the concern" is RAID 10.

title: Power supplies: wattage, rails, and connectors
summary: Sizing a PSU and the connectors you have to recognize.
body:
## Power supplies: sizing, connectors, and diagnosing them

The PSU converts wall AC into the DC rails every component needs. It is also a common source of symptoms that look like something else entirely, which is why it earns its own lesson.

### What the wattage rating means

The rating is the **maximum sustained output**, not what the machine draws. A 750 W supply in a system pulling 300 W is running at 40% load, which is fine — most units are most efficient somewhere near half load.

Size a supply by adding up the real consumers, then leaving headroom:

- The **graphics card** is usually the largest single draw in a desktop, often more than the rest of the system combined.
- The **CPU** is next.
- Drives, fans, and RAM are comparatively small.

Headroom matters for two reasons: transient spikes (a GPU can draw far above its average for brief moments), and future upgrades. Undersizing produces one of the most misleading fault patterns in the whole exam: **a system that is stable at idle and reboots or shuts down under load**, because demand momentarily exceeds what the supply can deliver.

### Efficiency ratings

**80 PLUS** certification (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Titanium) describes how much input power reaches the components rather than becoming heat. A higher rating means less waste heat, lower running cost, and usually better internal components — but it says nothing about capacity. An 80 PLUS Titanium 450 W unit is still a 450 W unit.

### Rails and connectors

Modern supplies distribute power over **+12 V**, **+5 V**, and **+3.3 V** rails, with +12 V doing most of the work for CPU and GPU.

| Connector | Feeds |
|---|---|
| **24-pin ATX** | The motherboard |
| **4/8-pin EPS (CPU)** | Supplementary CPU power near the socket |
| **PCIe 6-pin / 6+2-pin / 12VHPWR** | Discrete graphics cards |
| **SATA power** | Drives and some accessories |
| **Molex** | Legacy peripherals and fans |
| **Berg** | Legacy floppy drives |

A very common build error is forgetting the **EPS/CPU connector**. The board is powered through the 24-pin, fans spin, lights come on — and the system never posts, because the CPU has no supplementary power.

**Modular** supplies let you attach only the cables you need, which improves airflow and tidiness. The one hard rule: **never mix modular cables between different PSU models or brands.** The pinouts on the PSU end are not standardised, and using the wrong cable can put voltage where a device expects ground and destroy hardware.

### Form factors and voltage

**ATX** is the standard desktop size; **SFX** is the small-form-factor equivalent for compact cases. Mounting is not interchangeable without an adapter bracket.

Some supplies have a **manual voltage selector switch** (115 V / 230 V). Setting it wrong is destructive: a 230 V supply set to 115 V and plugged into 230 V will typically fail immediately. Modern auto-switching supplies detect input voltage themselves and have no switch to get wrong.

### Diagnosing a suspect supply

Symptoms that point at power:

- No response at all when the power button is pressed.
- Random reboots or shutdowns, especially under load.
- The system posts intermittently, or only after several attempts.
- Audible coil whine, buzzing, or a burning smell.
- Fans twitch briefly and stop.

Tools, in escalating order:

- A **PSU tester** plugs into the 24-pin and reports whether each rail is present and within tolerance. Fast, but it tests the supply under almost no load.
- A **multimeter** measures actual voltages on a live connector, letting you check rails while the system is running and under load — which is where a marginal supply actually fails.
- **Substitution** with a known-good supply of adequate wattage remains the definitive test.

> Exam habit: "stable at idle, shuts down under load" is the signature of an inadequate or failing power supply — but confirm cooling as well, because thermal shutdown produces the same pattern. Both are load-correlated; check temperatures before condemning the PSU.

### Safety

The PSU is the one component a technician should not open. Its capacitors store a **lethal charge long after it is unplugged**, and there are no user-serviceable parts inside. A failed supply is replaced, never repaired. Standard practice is to unplug the unit and hold the power button for several seconds to discharge residual power before working inside the case.

title: Peripherals: printers, scanners, and what breaks on each
summary: Printer technologies and their tell-tale failure symptoms, plus scanner basics.
body:
## Peripherals and printers: the parts that physically wear out

Printers are the most mechanical device most technicians touch, and mechanical things fail in patterns. Learn the process each technology uses and the symptoms follow.

### The laser imaging process, in order

The exam tests this sequence directly, and several fault questions depend on knowing which step produces which defect:

1. **Processing** — the page is rendered into a bitmap in the printer's memory.
2. **Charging** — the photosensitive drum receives a uniform electrical charge.
3. **Exposing** — a laser writes the image by discharging specific points on the drum.
4. **Developing** — toner is attracted to the discharged areas, forming the image on the drum.
5. **Transferring** — toner moves from drum to paper.
6. **Fusing** — heat and pressure melt the toner permanently into the paper.
7. **Cleaning** — residual toner is scraped away, readying the drum for the next page.

Map faults onto that:

| Symptom | Stage at fault |
|---|---|
| Toner smears or rubs off the page | **Fusing** — not enough heat or pressure |
| Repeating marks at a regular interval down the page | Drum or roller damage — the interval equals its circumference |
| Vertical white streaks | Toner distribution, or debris in the light path |
| Entirely blank pages | Toner empty, or transfer failing |
| Ghosting — a faint repeat of a previous image | **Cleaning** stage leaving residual charge or toner |

That first row is a favourite. Toner that never bonded means the page came through without being fused, so investigate the fuser and whether it is reaching temperature — not the toner cartridge.

### Inkjet

Inkjets spray liquid ink through a print head. Their maintenance concerns are entirely different from laser:

- **Head cleaning** clears nozzles clogged by dried ink. This is the fix for banding and missing colours.
- **Head alignment** corrects text that looks doubled or fuzzy, typically after a cartridge change.
- **Ink drying out** is the characteristic failure of an inkjet that sits unused for weeks.

Note also that inkjets use **liquid** ink, so a printed page can smudge if handled immediately — that is normal behaviour, not the fusing fault it resembles on a laser.

### Thermal and impact printers

**Thermal** printers use heat-sensitive paper and a heating element — receipts and shipping labels. They have no ink at all. Faded output usually means the **heating element needs cleaning** or the paper is old, and the paper must be stored away from heat and sunlight or it darkens on its own.

**Impact** (dot matrix) printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper. Because the strike is physical, they are the only technology that can produce genuine **multi-part carbon forms** — which is exactly why they survive in logistics and some medical settings. Faded print means a worn **ribbon**; consistently missing dots in characters means damaged **print head pins**.

### 3D printers

The exam covers these lightly: material is deposited layer by layer from **filament** or cured from **resin**, on a **print bed** that usually must be level and often heated so the first layer adheres. Prints detaching mid-job point at bed levelling or adhesion.

### Maintenance is scheduled, not reactive

Each technology has routine service that prevents faults rather than fixing them:

| Technology | Routine maintenance |
|---|---|
| Laser | Replace toner; replace maintenance kit (fuser, rollers) at rated page counts; clean with an **ESD-safe toner vacuum** |
| Inkjet | Clean and align heads; replace cartridges; run the printer periodically |
| Thermal | Clean the heating element; replace paper; keep paper cool and dark |
| Impact | Replace ribbon; replace print head; replace platen and tractor feed parts |

**Never use a standard vacuum on toner.** Toner particles are fine enough to pass straight through an ordinary filter and back into the air, and the fine dust can generate a static discharge inside the vacuum. A toner-rated, ESD-safe vacuum is the correct tool.

### Feed problems

Paper jams and misfeeds usually come down to a short list: worn **pickup rollers** that can no longer grip a single sheet, incorrect **tray guide** adjustment, humidity causing sheets to stick together, or the wrong paper weight for the path. Multiple sheets feeding at once almost always means rollers or humidity; a sheet stopping partway means an obstruction or a sensor.

### Other peripherals worth naming

- **ADF** (automatic document feeder) for multi-page scanning; a **flatbed** handles books and fragile originals.
- **KVM switch** — one keyboard, video, and mouse shared across several computers.
- **Digitizer / signature pad** — converts physical input into digital coordinates.
- **Webcams, headsets, and microphones** — most "not working" tickets are the wrong default device selected in the OS sound or camera settings rather than a hardware failure.

> Exam habit: when a printer question describes a defect, name the stage of the process that produces it before considering which part to order. The stage points at the part.

title: Deploying and configuring a printer, before anything goes wrong
summary: Setup, drivers, sharing, security, and network scanning — the configuration side, distinct from later maintenance.
body:
## Installing a printer properly, so it does not become a ticket

Objective 3.7 is about deployment and configuration — distinct from the maintenance covered elsewhere. The exam asks how you *set one up*, and what you configure so it behaves in a shared environment.

### Connection methods

| Method | When it fits |
|---|---|
| **USB** | One user, one machine. Simplest, no network dependency. |
| **Ethernet** | Shared office printer. Reliable and the normal choice. |
| **Wi-Fi** | Where cabling is impractical; more variables to troubleshoot. |
| **Wi-Fi Direct / ad hoc** | Direct device-to-printer without joining a network. |
| **Bluetooth** | Short-range, typically mobile or portable printers. |

A network printer should always receive a **stable address**. Left on plain DHCP, its address can change after a lease expiry or a power outage, and every workstation pointing at the old address stops printing. Configure either a static address or, better, a **DHCP reservation** so the printer is managed centrally but always gets the same address.

### Drivers: PCL versus PostScript

Most printers accept one of two page description languages, and choosing between them is a real decision:

- **PCL** (Printer Command Language) — developed by HP, lighter weight, generally faster for ordinary office documents.
- **PostScript** — developed by Adobe, better at complex graphics, precise fonts, and colour fidelity. The usual choice for design and prepress work.

Installing the wrong driver produces garbled output, wrong fonts, or pages of raw code — a distinctive symptom worth recognising.

### Sharing the printer

There are two models:

- **Local sharing**: the printer attaches to one workstation, which shares it. Everyone else's jobs pass through that machine, so it must be powered on. Fine for two or three people, fragile beyond that.
- **Print server**: a dedicated server (or the printer's own internal server) manages the queue. Clients print to it directly, and no user workstation is a dependency.

The **spooler** holds jobs until the printer can accept them. A stuck spooler is the single most common shared-printer fault: jobs pile up, nothing prints, and the printer itself is fine. The fix is to stop the spooler service, clear the queued job files, and restart it.

### Configuration options the exam names

- **Duplex** — printing both sides. Worth enabling by default for cost and paper saving.
- **Collate** — keeps multi-copy sets in page order rather than grouping all page ones together.
- **Orientation** — portrait or landscape.
- **Quality / resolution** — draft versus best, trading speed and consumables against output.
- **Tray selection** — which paper source to draw from, useful where letterhead lives in one tray.

### Secured printing and access control

Three features appear specifically in the objectives:

- **Secure print / pull printing** — the job is held until the user authenticates at the device, typically with a PIN or badge. This solves the confidentiality problem of sensitive documents sitting in an output tray where anyone can read or take them.
- **Badging** — the user taps an ID card at the printer to release jobs, which also produces an audit trail of who printed what.
- **User authentication and audit logging** — restricting who may use the device, and recording usage for accounting or investigation.

### Network scan services

Modern multifunction devices scan as well as print, and the destination options are testable:

| Destination | What it needs |
|---|---|
| **Scan to email** | SMTP server address, port, and credentials configured on the device |
| **Scan to folder (SMB)** | A share path plus an account with write permission to it |
| **Scan to cloud** | An authenticated connection to the cloud storage service |

Scan-to-folder failures are almost always **permissions** — the service account the device uses cannot write to the target share — or a changed password on that account.

### After installation

Finish the job properly: **print a test page** to confirm end-to-end operation, **calibrate** if the device supports it (particularly for colour alignment), verify duplex and the correct tray, and **document** the printer's address, driver, and location so the next technician is not rediscovering it.

> Exam habit: distinguish deployment questions from maintenance questions. Driver choice, sharing model, secure print, and scan destinations are 3.7 deployment topics; rollers, fusers, and toner are maintenance.

title: Cloud models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and the shared responsibility line
summary: Who manages what, and where your responsibility starts.
body:
## Cloud models: who is responsible for what

Nearly every cloud question reduces to one thing — where the boundary sits between what the provider manages and what you manage.

### The three service models

| Model | Provider manages | You manage | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IaaS** | Hardware, virtualisation, networking, storage | OS, patching, runtime, applications, data | A rented virtual server |
| **PaaS** | All of the above plus OS and runtime | Your application code and data | A managed app hosting platform |
| **SaaS** | Essentially everything | Your data, users, and configuration | Hosted email, CRM |

Read it as a ladder: each step up hands more of the stack to the provider and leaves you with less to administer — and less control. That trade is the whole point.

The **shared responsibility model** formalises this. The line moves with the service model, but two things never leave you: **your data**, and **who has access to it**. A provider's certification does not make a misconfigured public storage bucket their problem.

> Exam habit: if a scenario asks who patches the guest operating system, the answer depends entirely on the model — you, under IaaS; the provider, under PaaS and SaaS.

### The four deployment models

| Model | Description |
|---|---|
| **Public** | Provider-owned infrastructure shared among many tenants |
| **Private** | Infrastructure dedicated to one organisation |
| **Hybrid** | Private and public connected, workloads moving between them |
| **Community** | Shared by several organisations with common concerns (regulatory, industry) |

**Hybrid** appears constantly, and its scenario is always the same shape: regulated or sensitive data must stay on infrastructure the organisation controls, while variable or non-sensitive workloads use public capacity — "cloud bursting" at peak. **Community** is narrower and easy to distinguish: several *different* organisations sharing because they face the same requirements, such as a group of hospitals or government agencies.

### The characteristics that define cloud

- **On-demand self-service** — provision resources yourself, without a purchase order or a human in the loop.
- **Rapid elasticity** — capacity grows and shrinks automatically with demand.
- **Scalability** — capacity can grow, whether automatically or by request.
- **Resource pooling / multitenancy** — many customers served from shared physical infrastructure.
- **Measured service** — usage is metered, which is what makes pay-as-you-go possible.
- **Broad network access** — reachable from anywhere over the network.

**Elasticity versus scalability** is a distinction the exam draws: scalability is the ability to grow; elasticity is growing *and shrinking automatically* in response to load. A seasonal retail spike is the elasticity scenario.

**Multitenancy** is worth understanding as both the economic engine and the risk. Sharing hardware is what makes cloud cheap; it is also why isolation failures — one tenant reaching another's data — are a genuine concern.

### Cloud file storage and synchronisation

**File synchronisation** keeps the same file consistent across a user's devices automatically, backed by cloud storage. Edit on a laptop, and the phone has it moments later.

Two consequences worth carrying:

- **Sync is not backup.** A file deleted or corrupted on one device syncs that deletion everywhere. Versioning and recycle-bin features mitigate this, but the mechanism itself is replication, not preservation.
- **Bandwidth and connectivity matter.** An initial sync of a large folder saturates a link, and offline devices show stale data until they reconnect.

### Virtual desktops

**VDI** (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) hosts user desktops centrally and streams the display to endpoints. Data stays in the data centre rather than on the device, which is attractive for security and for supporting thin clients — but it makes the network a hard dependency, and a VDI deployment with an unreliable link is worse than local desktops.

### Cost and connectivity trade-offs

Cloud converts capital expenditure into operating expenditure: no hardware purchase, but a recurring bill that scales with use. The failure mode is cost sprawl — resources provisioned on demand and never decommissioned.

And the obvious dependency deserves stating because the exam does test it: **cloud makes internet connectivity critical rather than optional**. An office that moves its file server to the cloud has made its ISP a single point of failure for the ability to work at all.

title: Virtualization concepts: hypervisors, VMs, and VDI
summary: What actually runs a virtual machine, and how VDI differs from just having a VM.
body:
## Virtualization: one machine pretending to be several

Virtualization abstracts the operating system from the physical hardware, so several isolated systems share one set of components. Everything else in this domain builds on that idea.

### The two hypervisor types

| Type | Runs on | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Type 1 ("bare metal")** | Directly on the hardware | Production servers and data centres |
| **Type 2 ("hosted")** | On top of a normal OS | Desktop testing, labs, running a legacy OS |

A Type 1 hypervisor has no host operating system underneath competing for resources, so it is faster and has a smaller attack surface. A Type 2 hypervisor is an application you install on Windows or macOS — far more convenient, with the host OS's overhead and vulnerabilities beneath it.

### What a host actually needs

Three requirements, in the order they bite:

- **CPU virtualization extensions** — Intel **VT-x** or AMD **AMD-V**. These let guest instructions execute natively instead of being emulated. They are frequently **disabled by default in UEFI/BIOS**, and that is the single most common reason a new VM refuses to start or will not run a 64-bit guest.
- **RAM** — each guest reserves its own memory allocation, and this is normally the first ceiling you hit. The host OS needs its share too; over-committing memory causes heavy swapping and misery.
- **Storage** — each guest has one or more virtual disks, and they grow.

CPU cores and network capacity matter, but memory is what usually limits how many guests a host can run.

### Snapshots

A **snapshot** captures a VM's state at a moment in time, so it can be rolled back. It is the reason virtualization is so useful for testing: apply a patch, test it, and if it breaks something, revert in seconds.

The critical caveat, tested regularly: **a snapshot is not a backup.** It lives with the VM, on the same storage. If the datastore fails or the VM is deleted, the snapshots go with it. Snapshots also degrade performance the longer they are retained, because the system must track every change since they were taken.

### Virtual networking modes

A guest's virtual network adapter runs in one of a few modes, and "the VM has no network but the host does" is nearly always this setting:

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Bridged** | The guest appears as its own device on the physical network, with its own address |
| **NAT** | The guest shares the host's address; outbound works, inbound needs forwarding |
| **Host-only** | The guest can reach the host and other guests, but not the wider network |
| **Internal / isolated** | Guests can reach each other only — no host, no network |

Choose bridged when the guest must be reachable by other machines; NAT when it just needs internet access; host-only or internal when isolation is the point, such as malware analysis.

### Why organisations virtualize

- **Consolidation** — many lightly loaded physical servers become guests on fewer hosts, cutting hardware, power, and cooling.
- **Isolation** — a compromised or crashed guest does not take its neighbours down.
- **Sandboxing** — run untrusted software in a disposable environment and revert afterwards.
- **Legacy support** — keep an application that requires an old OS running on modern hardware, without dedicating a physical machine to it.
- **Cross-platform testing** — one workstation tests several OS versions.
- **Rapid provisioning** — clone a prepared template instead of building from scratch.

### Client-side virtualization requirements

Beyond the CPU extensions and memory already covered, two practical points appear:

- **Security requirements** — a guest needs its own patching, its own antivirus, and its own place in the network design. It is a real machine in every respect that matters, and "it is only a VM" is not a security posture.
- **Network requirements** — a bridged guest consumes an address on the real network and is subject to the same firewall and NAC policies as any physical host.

### VDI, and where it differs

**VDI** takes the idea further: desktops run centrally in the data centre and users connect from thin clients or ordinary PCs. The appeal is that **data never leaves the data centre**, provisioning is centralised, and a lost endpoint holds nothing.

The costs are a heavy dependence on the network and on central capacity. If the link is down, nobody works — which is exactly the trade a question about VDI is usually probing.

> Exam habit: "VM will not start" or "cannot run a 64-bit guest" points at virtualization extensions disabled in firmware. "VM runs but has no network" points at the virtual adapter's mode. Two different settings, two different symptoms.

title: The six-step troubleshooting methodology
summary: The process A+ tests directly — in order, and why the order matters.
body:
## The troubleshooting methodology, and the two steps people skip

CompTIA has one official sequence. It appears on both Core 1 and Core 2, and the exam tests the *order* far more than the wording.

### The six steps

1. **Identify the problem.**
2. **Establish a theory of probable cause** — question the obvious first.
3. **Test the theory to determine the cause.**
4. **Establish a plan of action** to resolve the problem and implement the solution.
5. **Verify full system functionality** and, if applicable, implement preventive measures.
6. **Document** findings, actions, and outcomes.

### Step 1 is more than "ask what's wrong"

Identifying the problem has named sub-parts, and questions are built from them:

- **Gather information** and **question the user** — what exactly happens, and when did it start?
- **Identify symptoms** — observe them yourself rather than relying on the description.
- **Determine if anything has changed** — new software, a patch, a moved cable, a storm last night. This is the highest-yield question in troubleshooting, because most things that break were working until something changed.
- **Duplicate the problem if possible** — a fault you can reproduce is a fault you can verify you have fixed.
- **Approach multiple problems individually** — do not let two faults confuse each other.

Core 1 adds one more instruction that the exam does test: **back up before making changes**. If a step could destroy data, the backup comes first.

### The step candidates skip: test the theory

This is the most commonly examined trap in the entire methodology. A question describes a technician who has formed a reasonable theory and asks what to do **next**. The tempting answer is to implement the fix. The correct answer is to **test the theory first**.

Untested theories are guesses. Testing is what separates diagnosis from parts-swapping, and swapping parts on a hunch is how you end up having replaced three components without fixing anything.

The step also has a defined fork: if the theory is **confirmed**, determine the next steps to resolve. If it is **not confirmed**, establish a new theory **or escalate**. Escalation is a legitimate outcome, not a failure — recognising that something is beyond your access or expertise is part of the process.

### Question the obvious

Step 2 explicitly says to question the obvious, and the exam rewards it. Before theorising about a failed motherboard, confirm the machine is plugged in, the monitor is on the right input, and the cable is seated. It sounds trivial; it is genuinely the resolution to a large share of real tickets.

Two structured approaches are named for narrowing a fault:

- **Top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top** through the OSI layers — usually bottom-up, because a physical fault explains every failure above it.
- **Divide and conquer** — test at the middle of the chain, and whichever half proves faulty gets divided again.

### Verify, then document

**Verification** means confirming the whole system works, not just that the original symptom is gone. Replacing a network card fixes connectivity — but did the printer mapping survive? Did the user's drive mappings come back? Preventive measures belong here too: if the cause was a dust-clogged cooler, cleaning it now prevents the repeat.

**Documentation is last, and it is not optional.** It records what the symptom was, what the cause turned out to be, and what fixed it. Its value is entirely to the next person — including you in six months — and it feeds the knowledge base that stops the same fault being diagnosed from scratch every time.

### Why the order is the point

Each step exists because skipping it causes a specific failure:

| Skip this | And you get |
|---|---|
| Identify the problem | Fixing the wrong thing |
| Establish a theory | Random parts swapping |
| **Test the theory** | Expensive guessing |
| Plan of action | Collateral damage from an unplanned change |
| Verify functionality | A callback for the thing you broke |
| Document | The same diagnosis repeated forever |

> Exam habit: when a question gives you a technician mid-process and asks for the next step, locate exactly where they are in the six steps and give the very next one. Do not jump ahead to the fix, and do not skip verification to get to documentation.

title: Reading POST failures and boot problems
summary: Beeps, no-POST, and where a boot actually dies.
body:
## When the machine will not boot: reading POST

POST — the Power-On Self-Test — runs before any operating system exists. That is what makes its output so useful: anything POST reports is hardware or firmware, with the OS entirely out of the picture.

### The boot sequence

1. Power is applied and the PSU asserts "power good."
2. The CPU begins executing firmware (UEFI or legacy BIOS).
3. **POST** tests essential hardware — CPU, memory, and basic video.
4. Firmware locates a boot device according to the configured boot order.
5. The bootloader loads, and the operating system starts.

Faults before step 5 are firmware and hardware territory. Faults after it are operating system territory — a distinction the exam relies on.

### How POST reports failure

**Beep codes** are the machine's only voice before video works. The pattern is vendor-specific, so the correct action is to consult that board's documentation rather than recite a universal table. Broadly: memory and video failures are the most common beeping faults, and a single short beep almost always means POST passed.

**POST codes** are two-character hexadecimal codes shown on a small onboard display or an add-in POST card, reporting exactly which test was executing when things stopped. Many modern boards instead use **diagnostic LEDs** labelled CPU, DRAM, VGA, and BOOT — whichever stays lit is the stage that failed, which is far easier than decoding beeps.

### The classic no-boot patterns

| Symptom | Most likely causes | First actions |
|---|---|---|
| Completely dead, no fans, no lights | PSU, power cable, wall outlet, front-panel switch | Confirm power, test/substitute PSU |
| Fans spin, no video, no beeps | RAM, GPU, CPU power connector not attached | Reseat RAM and GPU, confirm the EPS/CPU connector |
| Repeating beep pattern | Memory or video, per vendor code | Look up the code, reseat RAM |
| POSTs but "no boot device found" | Drive not detected, boot order changed, UEFI/Legacy mismatch | Check drive in firmware, check boot order and mode |
| Boots intermittently | Marginal PSU, loose connection, thermal issue | Reseat everything, test PSU under load |
| Continuous reboot loop | Overheating, failing PSU, faulty RAM | Check temperatures, test with one RAM module |

The **"fans spin but nothing happens"** case deserves attention because it feels like a dead board and usually is not. The three cheap things to check, in order, are the **CPU power connector** (the 4/8-pin EPS, easy to forget on a new build), the **memory** (reseat, or test one module at a time in the primary slot), and the **graphics card** seating. Strip to essentials — one RAM stick, no drives, no add-in cards — and see whether it posts.

### After a power outage

A machine that will not boot following an outage or a CMOS battery failure has a distinctive cause: **firmware settings reset to defaults**. That commonly changes the **boot order**, or flips the boot mode between **UEFI and Legacy/CSM**. A drive installed under UEFI with a GPT partition table simply will not be found in Legacy mode, and the machine reports no boot device while the drive is perfectly healthy.

A dying **CMOS battery** produces a recognisable trio: the clock resets, firmware settings revert, and the machine may complain about configuration on every start.

### Distinguishing hardware from software

The dividing line is whether the machine gets through POST:

- Fails **before** POST completes — hardware or firmware. The OS is not involved and reinstalling it will not help.
- Fails **after** POST, while loading the OS — boot files, drivers, corrupted system files, or a failing drive.

That is why "no boot device found" and "Windows failed to start" are entirely different problems despite both meaning "it will not boot." The first says firmware cannot find anything to load; the second says it found and started loading something that then failed.

### Storage failure warnings

A drive that is failing rather than failed announces itself: **S.M.A.R.T. warnings** at boot, clicking or grinding from a mechanical drive, files that intermittently fail to open, and long unexplained freezes while the system waits on I/O.

The response is always the same order: **get the data off first**, then replace the drive. Running repair utilities repeatedly against a physically dying drive adds wear and risks the data you have not copied yet.

> Exam habit: beep codes and diagnostic LEDs are pre-video reporting, so they always indicate hardware. If a scenario has the machine beeping or showing a DRAM LED, no amount of operating system work is the answer.

title: The physical troubleshooting toolkit
summary: Multimeter, cable tester, loopback plug — what each one actually proves.
body:
## The toolkit, and choosing the right instrument

Tool questions are usually phrased as a symptom plus "which tool," so what matters is knowing precisely what each one measures.

### Electrical instruments

| Tool | Measures | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Multimeter** | Voltage, current, resistance, continuity | Confirming PSU rails under load; checking a fuse or cable for continuity |
| **PSU tester** | Presence and rough tolerance of each rail | Quick pass/fail on a supply, with almost no load applied |
| **Power supply analyser** | Rail behaviour under applied load | Catching a supply that only fails when loaded |

The distinction between the last two matters: a PSU tester can pronounce a supply healthy when it collapses under real load. If the symptom is "stable at idle, dies under load," the tester is not sufficient evidence.

### Cable and network tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Cable tester (wiremap)** | Verifies each conductor end to end — opens, shorts, miswires, split pairs |
| **Cable certifier** | Confirms a run meets a category's full performance spec, not just continuity |
| **Tone generator and probe** | Traces which physical cable in a bundle is which |
| **Loopback plug** | Feeds a port's transmit back to its receive, testing the port itself |
| **Crimper** | Attaches connectors to cable ends |
| **Punchdown tool** | Seats conductors into a patch panel or keystone jack |
| **Wi-Fi analyser** | Shows channel usage, signal strength, and interference |
| **Network tap** | Copies traffic on a link for capture and analysis |

**Split pair** is the fault worth remembering here: two wires from different twisted pairs miswired together as one pair. The cable shows continuity and may even show a link light, but crosstalk destroys performance at higher speeds. A basic continuity check passes it; a proper wiremap tester catches it.

### Physical and safety equipment

- **Anti-static wrist strap and mat** — connect you and the workspace to the same potential so a discharge never passes through a component. Wear the strap connected to the chassis or a proper ground point.
- **ESD-safe toner vacuum** — the only correct way to clean spilled toner. A household vacuum blows the fine particles straight through its filter and can generate static internally.
- **Compressed air** — for dust, used in short bursts, with fans held so they cannot spin up and generate current.
- **Thermal paste and isopropyl alcohol** — replacing the thermal interface when a cooler is removed. The old paste must be cleaned off; alcohol and a lint-free cloth are the standard.
- **Screwdrivers, spudgers, and plastic pry tools** — plastic for opening laptop and phone housings, so you do not gouge or short anything.

### Electrostatic discharge

ESD is the invisible hazard. A discharge far below the threshold you can feel — well under 1,000 volts — is enough to damage a component, sometimes not immediately but as a latent failure weeks later.

Controls, in order of importance:

1. **Equalise potential** — wrist strap connected to the chassis, or at minimum touch an unpainted metal part of the case before handling components.
2. **Anti-static bags** for storage and transport. Note that the bag protects what is *inside* it, and a component should be set on top of an anti-static mat, not on top of the bag.
3. **Humidity** — very dry air greatly increases static build-up.
4. **Handle boards by their edges**, never by the contacts or components.

One important exception: **do not wear a wrist strap when working inside a CRT monitor or a power supply**, both of which store lethal high voltages. There you want isolation, not a path to ground through your body. Neither should be opened by a technician at all.

### Safety and disposal

- **Unplug and discharge** before working inside a case — hold the power button for several seconds after unplugging.
- **Lift correctly**, bending at the knees, and get help for heavy equipment such as UPS units and CRTs.
- **Batteries, CRTs, and toner** are all regulated waste. They go to proper recycling, never in general rubbish. A **swollen lithium-ion battery** is removed from service immediately, never punctured, and disposed of through a battery recycler.
- **Consult the SDS** (Safety Data Sheet) for any chemical — cleaning solvents, toner — for handling, first aid, and disposal instructions.

> Exam habit: a question naming a specific measurement usually names its tool. "Is this cable continuous?" is a cable tester. "Which of these cables is it?" is a toner and probe. "Is this port working?" is a loopback plug. "Is this rail at the right voltage under load?" is a multimeter.
